newsitem.title: DENMARK: FEATURE - Red Cross offers eastern Europe crisis partnership.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Red Cross offers eastern Europe crisis partnership.

text.p: The end of the Cold War has seen a huge increase in poverty and sickness in the former Soviet Union and eastern Europe and aid organisations say they will help the region to overcome the crisis.

The post-communist period in eastern Europe has seen vast changes with war, growing ethnic tension, social polarisation, youth drug abuse, violence and health and environmental problems, Joergen Poulsen, secretary-general of the Danish Red Cross, told Reuters.
Poulsen said these problems had been aggravated by decreasing public resources placing an ever escalating responsibility on humanitarian organisations.
"We tend to focus all the time on the European Union and forget that there is another Europe which lives in a completely different world.

"This other Europe has suffered a major breakdown since the collapse of the Iron Curtain. Over 50 million people in Russia and another 40 million in former Soviet bloc countries are living below the poverty line.
"We have a huge task ahead of us in holding these nations together. We want to offer them a partnership," Poulsen said.
Poulsen was speaking as Europe's Red Cross and Red Crescent societies met in Copenhagen last week to discuss aid strategies.

The organisations say that diseases such as diptheria, typhoid and cholera have reappeared in eastern Europe. In the former Soviet Union heart disease and suicide is becoming more common and life expectancy for the average male fell from 65 to 58 between 1989 and 1994.

"In many countries the heath system has totally collapsed and the Red Cross has to fill the gaps. The national societies must find a joint strategy in the fight against the new Europe's diseases," said Freddy Karup Pedersen, acting president of the Danish Red Cross.
"We must be ready to provide emergency aid but we must also hold governments to their duty to guarantee the health of citizens at national and international levels."
ALBANIAN CRISIS

"Europe is changing dramatically. It has more democracy than before but it has become less stable," the Red Cross and Red Crescent societies said in a declaration at the end of their four-day conference.
"There is less fear of an international war, yet the individual feels more insecure," they added.

The Albanian Red Cross, unable to attend the conference, sent a message to the 400 delegates describing the extensive plundering and destruction of its stores, offices and supply depots in the current unrest.

"The violence has not only involved robbery, arson and the destruction of economic, financial, social and administrative institutions, it has also left many dead and hundreds wounded," the message said.
The Geneva-based International Committee of the Red Cross appealed to donors to raise $10 milllion to finance emergency aid for the beleaguered Balkan country.
POVERTY WIDESPREAD
Poverty is a vast problem. The Red Cross estimates that more than half of the Bulgarian population is living below the poverty line.

"Abject poverty reigns in former Soviet countries, people are dying of starvation, the lifespan is falling, child deaths are more frequent than ever before, old illnesses we thought were eradicated are spreading there," Poulsen said.
"It would be dangerous not to help these countries overcome their catastrophic problems, we must help them to functiion better, to enable them to become more democratic."
The conference was the first time that Red Cross and Red Crescent societies from both sides of the old ideological divide in Europe had met since the fall of the Iron Curtain.
It ended with the signing of more than 100 cooperation and partnership agreements between 50 Red Cross and Red Crescent societies from Europe and the former Soviet Union.
"I am optimistic that we can weld eastern and western Europe together through an active humanitarian partnership in the fight against poverty," said Poulsen.
